Neighboring hexagons share an edge, every node has two or three neighbors, and there are no triangles." width="100%"} Creates a honeycomb of `rows` rows with `cols` hexagons in each, the same lattice as NetworkX's `hexagonal_lattice_graph(rows, cols)`. It's built as a "brick wall": the nodes sit in `cols + 1` columns of `2 * rows + 2`, each column is a path, and node `(row, col)` is joined to `(row, col + 1)` when `row + col` is even. The two corner nodes that would hang off the wall by a single edge are left out, so the lattice has `2 * (rows * cols + rows + cols)` nodes. Every node has two or three neighbors, and the bounded faces are six-cycles: drawn with each column zigzagging, they are regular hexagons. The graph is bipartite and planar. Each node is labelled with its zero-based position as `"(row,col)"`, and nodes are created row by row. In a directed graph every edge points to the right within a row or to the next row. The lattice is appended without touching or connecting to existing nodes, and the whole construction is recorded as a single step. Hexagonal lattices are useful for: - modeling honeycomb structures: graphene and other two-dimensional materials, and hexagonal cell layouts in wireless networks - spatial simulations on a lattice with three neighbors per site (percolation and spin models) - test cases for bipartite, planar, sparse graphs with long cycles and no triangles ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [rows]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of rows of hexagons. Must be at least `1`. [cols]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of hexagons in each row. Must be at least `1`. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `type` attribute of every new node. If `None` (default), no `type` attribute is set. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), each node is labelled with its position as `"(row,col)"`. Because these labels don't depend on the existing nodes, adding a second labelled lattice raises `ValueError` (labels are unique); pass `label=False` for the second one. If `False`, nodes are created without labels. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional value stored in the `rel` attribute of every new edge. If `None` (default), no `rel` attribute is set. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. The graph is modified in place. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `rows=` or `cols=` is less than `1`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} One row of two hexagons has ten nodes and eleven edges, since the hexagons share an edge. The shortest cycle has six edges: ::: {#8886c40a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_hexagonal_lattice_graph(rows=1, cols=2) graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges(), graph.girth() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (10, 11, 6) ``` ::: ::: A larger honeycomb has no triangles at all, and no node has more than three neighbors: ::: {#c3418815 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} honeycomb = ec.Graph().add_hexagonal_lattice_graph(rows=4, cols=5) len(honeycomb.list_triangles()), honeycomb.get_node_df()["degree"].max() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (0, 3) ``` ::: :::
